mechanism.rule: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Walk-In Coolers and Walk-In Freezers (final rule, RIN 1904-AD79, docket EERE-2017-BT-STD-0009)
mechanism.agency: Department of Energy (Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy)
mechanism.required: DOE adopted amended energy conservation standards for walk-ins and said they would save significant energy and were technologically feasible and economically justified. The rule did not amend standards for display doors or panels. It set maximum daily energy consumption standards for walk-in non-display doors and higher minimum efficiency standards (AWEF2) for walk-in refrigeration systems. Non-display doors had to comply by December 23, 2027, and refrigeration systems by December 31, 2028. The standards would have applied to manufacturers of this equipment. For walk-in panels, DOE did not adopt more stringent standards.
mechanism.benefits: DOE's own analysis, in the final rule: the cumulative net present value of total consumer benefits is $2.00 billion (7% discount rate) to $4.74 billion (3% discount rate). The analysis period is equipment purchased in 2029–2058 for refrigeration systems and 2028–2057 for non-display doors. National energy savings were projected at 1.60 quads (full-fuel-cycle). DOE described this as a 6.3 percent saving relative to energy use without amended standards. Cumulative emission reductions over the same period were estimated at 28.82 million metric tons of CO2, plus 8.8 thousand tons of SO2 and other pollutants. Annualized, at a 3% discount rate: $369.8 million per year in reduced equipment operating costs, $96.5 million in climate benefits and $189.4 million in health benefits, for a net benefit of $554.5 million per year. All figures are DOE's, in 2023 dollars, and cover equipment shipped over the analysis period.
mechanism.costs: DOE's own analysis, from the same final rule. At a 3% discount rate, the estimated cost is $101.2 million per year in increased equipment costs. At a 7% rate for consumer costs, the estimated cost is $99.1 million per year in increased equipment costs. For manufacturers, the technical support document states the change in industry net present value (INPV) for walk-ins ranges from -$63 million to -$42 million. Official dispute: No CBO, GAO or court finding disputing DOE's estimates was found. The GAO major-rule report restates DOE's NPV figures without assessing them.
mechanism.agency_reasons: Under EPCA, DOE must periodically review its existing standards to determine whether more-stringent standards would be technologically feasible and economically justified, and would result in significant energy savings. DOE concluded the adopted standards represent the maximum improvement in energy efficiency that is technologically feasible and economically justified, and would result in significant conservation of energy.
mechanism.sponsor_reasons: Rep. Stephanie Bice (R-OK), the House sponsor, said overturning the rule protects economic freedom and consumer choice and keeps businesses from bearing unnecessary costs. She also described the rule as having an estimated compliance cost of nearly $1 billion. Her floor remarks said the resolution would protect small businesses from unnecessary compliance cost and preserve the diversity of choice available to consumers. In a release quoted on Bice's site, Chairwoman McClain said the regulations limited consumer choice, raised prices, and put unnecessary financial burdens on American businesses and families. House Energy and Commerce Chairmen Guthrie and Latta said the rule was an example of needless regulation raising prices for businesses and families while failing to provide cost savings or increase food safety. Rep. Fedorchak said the rule was neither technologically feasible nor economically justified (her characterization). Industry groups NACS, the National Grocers Association and FMI sent a letter supporting the resolution; they said retailers would have to absorb costs or pass them to consumers as higher prices. DOE's own annualized equipment-cost estimates are roughly $99–101 million per year ($99.1 million and $101.2 million). The DOE technical support document reports a present-value consumer incremental product cost of $0.96 billion at a 7% discount rate and $1.78 billion at 3%.
mechanism.status: Became law. H.J.Res. 24 passed the House on 2025-03-27 and the Senate on 2025-04-03. It was sent to the President on May 5, 2025 and signed on May 9, 2025. As Public Law 119-7, Congress disapproves the rule at 89 Fed. Reg. 104616, and the rule has no force or effect. The rule is void. DOE had earlier delayed its effective date twice (90 FR 9951 on 02/20/25 and 90 FR 13054 on 03/20/25). It then published a withdrawal notice (90 FR 21391) on 05/20/25.

outcomes.claim: DOE delayed the rule's effective date twice, on 02/20/25 (90 FR 9951) and 03/20/25 (90 FR 13054). It then published a withdrawal on 05/20/25 (90 FR 21391). The Unified Agenda entry states that the rule no longer has force or effect.

Benefit forgone, per DOE's pre-vote analysis. DOE estimated the standards would have delivered cumulative consumer net present value of $2.00 billion (7% discount rate) to $4.74 billion (3%) for walk-in non-display doors purchased 2028–2057 and walk-in refrigeration systems purchased 2029–2058. It also projected 1.60 quads of full-fuel-cycle energy savings and 28.82 Mt of CO2 reductions over the same period. The annualized net benefit at a 3% discount rate was $554.5 million per year, including $369.8 million in operating-cost savings. This is a forecast made before the vote, not a measured result.

source.title: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Walk-In Coolers and Walk-In Freezers (final rule)

outcomes.counterpoint: In the same analysis DOE estimated increased equipment costs of $99.1–$101.2 million per year. DOE's manufacturer INPV change was -$61.2 million to -$45.7 million for refrigeration systems and -$2.0 million to +$3.5 million for non-display doors. Sponsors said the cost was nearly $1 billion, and that figure could not be traced to the DOE pages reviewed. No CBO, GAO or court finding disputing DOE's estimates was found. DOE's climate and health benefit values depend on its chosen social-cost and discount-rate assumptions.

outcomes.claim: Cost burden projected by DOE in the final rule. DOE estimated that the walk-in cooler and freezer standards adopted in this rule would increase equipment costs by $99.1 million per year at a 7% discount rate and $101.2 million per year at 3%. Compliance would be required starting December 23, 2027, and December 31, 2028, depending on the equipment class.

source.title: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Walk-In Coolers and Walk-In Freezers (final rule)

outcomes.counterpoint: DOE's same analysis projected that operating-cost savings ($304.4–$369.8 million per year) would exceed these added equipment costs. It also said non-display door standards could be met with existing equipment. How much of the cost would have been passed on to customers was not established in the sources I opened.

outcomes.claim: The Appliance Standards Awareness Project (ASAP), an efficiency advocacy group, said after the Senate vote that blocking the standards would raise costs for restaurants, convenience stores and grocery stores, and that those costs would be passed on to consumers. It said bill savings would repay the added upfront cost within 1.6 years on average for non-display doors and 3 years on average for refrigeration systems. ASAP's release also cites a Department of Energy estimate that the standards would save businesses up to $6.5 billion on utility bills over 30 years of product sales. These are projections made at the time of the vote. No measurement of actual price or bill changes was found.

source.title: Senate Vote to Undo Efficiency Standards for Walk-In Coolers Will Raise Bills, Strain Electric Grid

outcomes.counterpoint: ASAP is an advocacy organization, and its payback figures are projections, not records of events.
outcomes.quote: will raise costs for restaurants, convenience stores, and grocery stores—costs that will be passed on to consumers

notes: (1) No credible record of measured effects on people was found. I found no agency data, GAO or inspector-general report, or peer-reviewed study of how equipment prices, business costs, energy use or food prices changed after the repeal. The standards' compliance dates (Dec. 2027 and Dec. 2028) fall after the period I could check, so real-world effects would not be visible yet. That is a valid finding, not a gap to fill with forecasts. (2) The DOE figures (NPV, annualized benefits and costs, INPV) are DOE's forecasts, published before the vote. They are estimates, not documented outcomes. The 7% annualized case was truncated in the text I opened, so I did not report its health-benefit or net-benefit figures. Ballotpedia lists an estimated benefit of $672.7 million and cost of $99.1 million, but I did not rely on it because it is a secondary source. (3) The sponsors' 'nearly $1 billion' compliance-cost figure was not located in the DOE final-rule pages or the TSD summary I opened. It may refer to a different measure, such as total conversion or lifetime costs. I have recorded it as the sponsors' statement and have not verified it. (4) The Conference Board noted at the time that it was unclear whether rollbacks would change the equipment manufacturers actually produce. Many manufacturers may already have been moving toward the higher levels (reported in a policy alert, not an official analysis). (5) H.J.Res. 24 is one of several DOE appliance-standard CRA resolutions signed together on May 9, 2025. Outcomes specific to this rule are hard to separate from the others. (6) Sources and what I opened: the Federal Register, GAO, Congress.gov, the Public Law text and the Unified Agenda entries were opened. Other items (press releases, ASAP, trade-press articles) are used only for statements of reasons and projections, not as evidence of outcomes. (7) The CRA's bar on reissuing a 'substantially the same' rule is part of the statute. I did not open a source on its effect here, so I have made no claim about whether DOE may issue a new walk-in standard.
